void-architecture.title: Infrastructure and Performance: From Concept to Production
void-architecture.summary: How I built a high-performance system using Bun, Go, and Podman on minimalist infrastructure.

content.podman_title: The infrastructure: VPS, Podman, and Nginx
content.podman_content:
Operating a high-performance system on an infrastructure with 70GB of SSD, 2vCPUs, and 4GB of RAM requires more than just clean code; it requires a surgical infrastructure strategy. In this scenario, every CPU cycle and every megabyte of RAM are treated as precious resources. The decision to use Podman over traditional Docker was the first critical step in this optimization journey.

The main point here isn't just to run this portfolio. My real and ambitious goal is to HOST ALL existing and future projects on this same infrastructure. I am talking about a complete ecosystem running under the same constraints. That's why every bit matters, every idle process is an enemy, and every optimization is a strategic victory to ensure the machine supports the growth of my entire application portfolio.

A decision that might seem controversial to container purists is using Nginx directly on the host, rather than via a container. The reason? Raw performance and routing simplicity. By running Nginx natively, I eliminate any additional network layer or bridge that Podman might introduce, ensuring response times are the lowest physically possible. Furthermore, as Nginx is my 'front door' for ALL projects residing on this VPS, having it on the host drastically simplifies managing SSL certificates via Certbot and dynamic routing to different containers, without the complexity of cross-container internal networks.

Podman shines because it is daemonless. While Docker requires a central process running with root privileges all the time, consuming resources even when idle, Podman operates much more directly, integrating natively with systemd. This not only reduces the attack surface through rootless containers but also allowed me to achieve corporate-level isolation and security without sacrificing the meager available memory, allowing my VPS to breathe better and focus processing on what really matters: the stable execution of multiple simultaneous projects.
content.ci_cd_content:
In a project that values precision, manual deployment is a cardinal sin. Therefore, I implemented a completely automated production line using GitHub Actions. Each commit to the main branch triggers a symphony of events: the code is validated, artifacts are built (whether the Go binary or the React bundle), and deployment is executed directly to my VPS via SSH, silently and efficiently.

But automation doesn't stop at deployment. Dependabot acts as a tireless sentinel, watching over every library and dependency in my ecosystem. It not only warns me about vulnerabilities but opens automatic pull requests that are tested by my CI pipelines. This allows me to keep the project always at the state of the art in security and performance, without the burden of exhaustive manual maintenance.

This culture of automation allows the focus to remain where it really matters: on product evolution. Knowing that the infrastructure is capable of self-managing and that the update process is robust gives me the creative freedom necessary to test new ideas, knowing that the 'sentinel' is always watching for any potential instability or technical debt that may arise.
content.performance_content:
When I talk about performance, Bun and Go are the undisputed protagonists. On the front-end side, Bun has completely revolutionized the way I work with the Javascript ecosystem. It not only accelerated build times from minutes to a few seconds but brought incredible cohesion to the toolkit, eliminating the need for multiple fragmented packages for testing, build, and execution.

On the back-end, the precision and sobriety of Go with the Fiber framework form the backbone of the system. I chose Go for its legendary ability to manage concurrency through goroutines with a tiny memory footprint. On a machine with 4GB of RAM that needs to support multiple projects, I cannot afford to run heavy runtimes that take time to release memory or that suffer from long Garbage Collection pauses.

The result of this combination is a system that responds in milliseconds and maintains linear stability, even under load. Go gives me the security of a typed system and execution speed close to C++, while Bun ensures that front-end development is agile and that the generated artifacts are as optimized as possible for the end-user's browser.
content.frontend_title: The front-end challenge (and the prompts kkk)
content.frontend_content:
I'll be honest with you: at the beginning of this project, my knowledge of how to implement complex animations on the front-end was practically zero. I had ambitious visual ideas, inspired by science fiction interfaces and high-performance dashboards, but I had no idea how to translate that into React code that was fluid and didn't destroy browser performance.

This is where the journey got interesting (and a bit frustrating kkk). It took MANY prompts, hundreds of trials and errors, and almost stubborn persistence to understand how Framer Motion and the React lifecycle work together. There were moments when a simple screen transition seemed like an impossible enigma, resulting in long conversations with the assistant and laughs of despair seeing the screen break in creative ways kkk.

However, the learning was transformative. Mastering the balance between 'Premium' aesthetics and technical performance was the big prize. Being able to keep Lighthouse at 100% while implementing glassmorphism effects, hover micro-interactions, and smooth transitions at 60fps was proof that, with the right help from prompts and a lot of insistence, it is possible to create interfaces that look 'magical' to the observer but are purely logical under the hood.
content.future_content:
This ecosystem is only in its initial phase. The horizon I envision involves the transition to more robust data persistence, but without losing my low-overhead philosophy. The next big step is SQLite integration. Far from being a 'toy' database, modern SQLite, configured with WAL mode and running on my fast SSDs, offers transactional performance that rivals much heavier client-server databases.

In addition to persistence, the future focus will be the creation of a true testing empire. The stability I have today is great, but I want it to be guaranteed by code, not by luck. The implementation of rigorous unit tests in the Go back-end and E2E (End-to-End) tests in the front-end will be my primary defense against regressions as I add new features and the system scales in complexity.

The idea is for this portfolio to become a personal engineering reference: a system that proves you don't need infinite cloud budgets or excessively complex microservices architectures to deliver a world-class product. It's about the elegance of simplicity and the power of continuous optimization. The future is light and fast.

Rust? será?
